facts.text: Latency is the delay between an event in front of a machine and the machine's reaction; in a braking system, latency spans sensing, the brake command and actual deceleration.
facts.quote: Latency is the delay between the moment something happens in front of the machine and the moment the machine reacts, measured in a braking system from sensing to the brake command and on to actual deceleration.

facts.text: End-to-end machine latency is the sum of sensor frame capture, detection and tracking, logic confirmation over several frames, network command transmission, brake-valve filling and brake-force build-up.
facts.quote: the sensor captures a frame, the computer detects and tracks, the logic waits a few frames to confirm the risk, the command crosses the network, the brake valves fill and the brake force builds. Only then does the machine slow. End-to-end latency is the sum.

facts.text: A machine continues moving during latency, losing distance according to d = v * t, where v is speed in meters per second and t is delay in seconds.
facts.quote: The machine keeps moving while it waits. The lost distance is speed times delay, `d = v * t`, with `v` in meters per second and `t` in seconds.

facts.text: At 15 km/h, approximately 4.2 m/s, a one-second latency adds 4.2 meters of travel before braking begins.
facts.quote: At 15 km/h (about 4.2 m/s) a one-second latency costs 4.2 meters before braking begins.

facts.text: At work-site speeds of 5 to 15 km/h, the booklet finds that latency can account for half or more of the whole stopping distance and is a first-order term.
facts.quote: The booklet finds that at 5 to 15 km/h the latency term can be half or more of the whole stopping distance, a first-order term at work-site speeds [Chapter 8].

facts.text: A published brake-response figure for a tracked vehicle is under 0.3 seconds.
facts.quote: Published brake-response figures range from under 0.3 s for a tracked vehicle

facts.text: A published brake-response figure for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire system is 0.41 seconds.
facts.quote: 0.41 s for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire

facts.text: A published brake-response figure for road air brakes is about 0.5 seconds.
facts.quote: about 0.5 s for road air brakes

facts.text: A United States mining regulation specifies brake-response figures of 0.5 to 2.5 seconds by weight class.
facts.quote: 0.5 to 2.5 s by weight class in a United States mining regulation

facts.text: Historic haul-truck retarders had a lag of 1 to 2 seconds.
facts.quote: historic haul-truck retarders lagged 1 to 2 s.

facts.text: Modern brake-response figures for production loaders, haulers and haul trucks were not found and must be measured.
facts.quote: Modern figures for production loaders, haulers and haul trucks were not found and must be measured [Chapter 8].

facts.text: ISO 16001, the international standard for object detection on earth-moving machines, caps detection time at 300 milliseconds.
facts.quote: ISO 16001, the international standard for object detection on earth-moving machines, caps detection time at 300 ms [Chapter 3].

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 treats detection, determination, action and machine stopping as separate portions of collision-system distance.
facts.quote: ISO 21815-3 treats detection, determination, action and machine stopping as separate portions of the collision-system distance [Chapters 8, 9].

facts.text: One South African regime requires detection of a lost connection within 500 milliseconds.
facts.quote: One South African regime requires a lost connection to be detected within 500 ms

facts.text: One South African regime requires the machine to reply within 50 milliseconds.
facts.quote: One South African regime requires a lost connection to be detected within 500 ms and the machine to reply within 50 ms [Chapter 7].

facts.text: The booklet calculates required detection distance as speed multiplied by the sum of detection, decision and actuation times, plus physical stopping distance and a margin.
facts.quote: The booklet's formula writes the required detection distance as speed times the sum of detection, decision and actuation times, plus the physical stopping distance and a margin [Chapter 9].

facts.text: Disagreement between two recorders' clocks can create an apparent algorithm latency of 100 to 300 milliseconds that is entirely a timestamp offset.
facts.quote: if two recorders' clocks disagree, an apparent "algorithm latency" of 100 to 300 ms can be nothing but a timestamp offset [Chapter 7].

facts.text: The booklet recommends end-to-end latency tests that inject a known object event and timestamp every stage from detection to measurable deceleration.
facts.quote: The booklet asks for end-to-end tests that inject a known object event and timestamp every stage from detection to measurable deceleration [Chapter 8].

facts.text: The first prototype tests should measure end-to-end latency, detection range and brake timing before any large scenario sweep, because incorrect values can make millions of virtual runs produce false confidence.
facts.quote: The first tests on the prototype should measure end-to-end latency, detection range and brake timing before any large scenario sweep, because if these numbers are wrong, millions of virtual runs produce false confidence [Chapter 1].
